newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Thailand, Korea in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Thailand, Korea in spotlight.

text.p: Thailand and South Korea hogged the debt market spotlight on Tuesday -- as one unveiled a package to revive a shattered economy and the other was warned its sovereign credit rating might be cut.
Thailand approved a series of measures to revive the economy and obtain US$12 billion to US$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The measures included suspending more than half of Thailand's 91 finance firms, setting targets for its foreign exchange reserves and cutting the current account deficit.

But bankers said they would wait to gauge public reaction to the package, while one Hong Kong-based bond fund manager questioned how readily the Thai public would accept what was likely to be an austerity package.
Another Thai corporate has missed an interest payment -- MDX Co Ltd failed to make a 57 million baht interest payment on debentures on July 30.
In other news, Korea's woes deepened on Tuesday with the news that Moody's Investors Service might cut its credit ratings.

Moody's said it was reviewing its Prime-1 foreign currency short term notes and bank deposit ratings, and its A-1 foreign currency rating for long term bank deposits, but affirmed its foreign currency bond rating.
The sovereign review means some ratings of Korea Development Bank, Industrial Bank of Korea, Housing & Commercial Bank and Export-Import Bank of Korea are also under review, Moody's said.
Among the factors cited in the review was Korea's increasing vulnerability to a near-term liquidity squeeze as a result of large and rapid buildup of short term debt in recent years.
Korea debt largely weathered the news, but bankers said investors have steadily been pushing up spreads since January when Hanbo collapsed after piling up 5 trillion won in debt.
For example, spreads over U.S. treasuries have widened by about 40 basis points over the year to date, with about 10 basis points of that coming in the last month.

Analysts also said spreads between state-owned banks like Korea Development Bank or Export-Import Bank of Korea and Korea First Bank have ballooned to about 120 basis points from 20 basis points over roughly the same period.
According to recent research from HSBC Markets, sovereign proxy Korea Development Bank (AA/A-1) was trading wider than China (BBB-plus/A-3) in late July, even though it was higher rated.
Traders saw room for wider spreads on quasi sovereign Korean bank one-year floating-rate debt by five to six basis points.
Regardless of the outcome of the Moody's review, the Hong Kong-based fund manager said Korea was already having to accept a higher cost of funding -- a "Korea premium".
"They're obliged to keep on issuing. They have a large funding programme so the supply of (debt) securities has to keep coming. It's just a question of pricing," he said.
Guangzhou-Shenzhen Superhighways Holdings Ltd had its two-tranche US$600 million bond priced in New York overnight.
The seven year US$200 million tranche went at 375 basis points over the underlying treasuries, and the 10 year US$400 million tranche went at 412.5 basis points over.
